content.thinking:
I'm noticing a timing discrepancy — the flag evaluation log shows the feature toggled at 15:16, but the official change record timestamps the event at 15:21:33Z, which seems to actually mark when the alert fired rather than when the flag changed.

The mitigation action itself looks inconclusive too: the revert was marked as "withdrawn" rather than confirmed, and the check at 15:22:02 only happened nine seconds after the human resolved it, so there isn't solid evidence that reverting the flag actually restored service.

Looking at the rollout data, the flag was partially enabled at 15:16 (80 of 200 evaluations on), with elevated error rates and several occurrences during the 15:17–15:21 window. As for why the flag caused a ZeroDivisionError at spend_summary.py line 47, the record doesn't explain the underlying division-by-zero logic itself, but it does establish that the mechanism was the flag enabling a code path that triggers that error — so I'd say the chain does reach a causal explanation at that level, even without deeper code visibility.

I also note some noise: a client disconnection error appears tied to a pre-existing baseline and looks benign, and there's an odd warning value that seems anomalous and not worth dwelling on. Going forward I need to reference figures using their labeled placeholders rather than writing out actual numbers.

Contributing factors include no staged rollout or error-rate guard, no pre-enable test, and a change-event lookup that returned zero prior changes since the event was logged after onset -- plus a short verification window and manual resolution after the action was withdrawn. For action items, I'll number them sequentially since the record has none, proposing fixes like correcting the division error with a regression test, adding rollout gating with an error-rate guard, ensuring flag-change events are recorded and indexed promptly, and defining mitigation steps.

I also note mitigation wasn't actually shown to restore service -- Argus was only checked once at T19, so the incident appears closed without confirmed recovery, meaning the executive summary should reflect at least that duration as unresolved. I'm now drafting the causal chain: first the symptom of failed account pages with elevated error rates citing the relevant alert, then the immediate cause of a ZeroDivisionError at a specific code line with its occurrence count, and I'm working through why that code path gets triggered in the first place.

The path only activates when the monthly-spend feature flag is on, which started evaluating at a specific timestamp; the flag was switched on by an admin, and I'm ruling out deploys or pre-existing baseline errors as causes since there's only one flag change in the history. I note the division-by-zero root cause itself isn't explained by the available records, so I'll stop the chain there and flag the timing discrepancy between when the flag change was recorded versus when evaluations actually began as an assumption worth calling out.

For lessons learned, I'm considering that the flag was only partially rolled out (a fraction of total instances), which may have limited the blast radius somewhat luckily, though I want to be careful not to overstate this since peak error counts don't equal total impact -- I'll keep the point that having a flag-based revert path was a saving grace.

action_items.item: Fix the division by zero at src/io_shop/spend_summary.py:47, working out which divisor is zero. Add a test for that case before monthly-spend-feature is enabled again.
Roll out flags like monthly-spend-feature in stages, with an automatic switch-off if the error rate on the affected page rises above its baseline.
Make flag toggles appear in the production change events promptly, with the time of the actual toggle, so the change lookup for the window before an onset includes them.

After a mitigation such as a flag revert, re-check the service over a longer window before judging the action or resolving the incident. Record whether the error rate recovered, and do not close the incident as resolved while the check still shows the incident's level.
Add an alert or annotation that fires when the error rate on a page rises soon after a flag change on that service, so it does not depend only on the paging rule's wait.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers saw account page requests fail. The error rate rose from {errors_before} to an average of {errors_while_broken} and peaked at {errors_at_worst}, and the paging alert fired {alert_raised - began} after the onset.

The failing requests raised ZeroDivisionError (division by zero) at src/io_shop/spend_summary.py:47. These errors began in the first minute of the incident and kept recurring until the logs were read.

The spend summary path runs only when monthly-spend-feature is on. Flag evaluations show it on from the onset, with {G971b.3} of {G971b.4} evaluations on in the first minute, and still on in later minutes.

An admin switched monthly-spend-feature on, a flag-toggle change. Other candidates were ruled out. The change lookup read {T9.2} deploys or releases in the day before the onset, so no earlier change explains it. The flag provider's history showed {T14.2} recent flag change, which was this one. The ClientDisconnected errors from shoppers closing connections were already present before the onset, so they are baseline noise.
The record does not show why the code at spend_summary.py:47 divides by zero, for example which divisor was zero or why no test caught it. The evidence stops here.

contributing_factors.factor: The flag was switched on for live traffic and the broken path took effect at once. No pre-enable test of the spend summary path and no error-rate guard on the rollout were seen in the record.

The flag-toggle change is recorded at {P1.1}, after the onset, and the change lookup before the onset read {T9.2} changes. The trigger was therefore not visible as a change when Argus looked, and it was found only through the flag provider's history.

The mitigation check ran shortly after the flag revert, saw the service still at the incident's level, and withdrew the action. The incident was then resolved by hand without a recovery confirmed in the record, so it is unknown whether the revert worked.

The paging rule waits {rule_waits} with its condition holding before it fires. Part of the {alert_raised - began} from onset to alert is that built-in wait, but no earlier signal tied the error rise to the flag change.

input.executive_summary: Shoppers on the io-shop account page got errors. The error rate was {errors_before} before the onset. It averaged {errors_while_broken} while the service was broken and peaked at {errors_at_worst}, so about {errors_rise} of traffic failed that would otherwise have worked. The service was broken for at least {duration}; that is a lower bound, because it had not recovered when the incident was closed. The trigger was a feature flag for a new monthly spend summary being switched on, which exposed a division-by-zero error. Argus reverted the flag, but its check shortly afterwards still saw the service at the incident's level, so it judged the action withdrawn. A person then closed the incident, kept the flag off and told the checkout team. The record does not show the service recovering.

went_well: Argus started investigating within seconds of the alert, placed the onset at 15:16 and found the flag as the single leading candidate.
The logs gave a specific error and location, ZeroDivisionError at spend_summary.py:47, which tied the failures to the flag-gated path.
The mitigation was a quick flag revert, and it was judged honestly as withdrawn when the service still looked unrecovered.
went_wrong: The service was broken for at least {duration}, and the record does not show it recovering.
The incident was marked resolved while the revert had not been shown to work.
The flag change was not visible in the change lookup before the onset, so the trigger was identified from logs and flag history rather than from change events.

input.root_cause: Switching on the monthly-spend-feature flag sent account page requests down a spend summary code path that raises ZeroDivisionError at src/io_shop/spend_summary.py:47, so every request that took that path failed. The record does not show why the divisor was zero, and the code was not read or tested in this incident.
